title: Evidence-Grounded ASR Semantic Consequence Rubric
principles: Answer G1, G2, S1-S4, C1, and C2 independently. A semantic difference does not by itself determine recoverability or reader impact, and a visible surface difference does not by itself establish a semantic difference.

Interpret the aligned edit in the complete sentence. Keep alignment boundary quality separate from content. When adjacent or repeated material completes the apparent fragment, or the spans select different neighboring units, do not infer truncation from the isolated spans; judge the resulting full expression. Punctuation, spacing, repetition, and spill are form effects unless the edit actually removes informative lexical or grammatical material.

A deletion within the same aligned lexical unit is a semantic or item difference when it leaves an informative word, predicate, name, technical term, identifier, or value incomplete and the hypothesis contains no complete recognized item. Contextual guessability is not full recovery. A proper-name spelling is a form variant only when it is an established rendering that still uniquely identifies the same entity, not merely because it is phonetically close.

Discourse markers, fillers, code-switched grammatical equivalents, conventional spoken forms, ordinary homophones in a uniquely constraining collocation, and grammatical ellipsis are form-only when the complete sentence still gives the same core claim and uniquely preserves the same participant. A change in a pronoun's person, number, possessor, or specific referent is a relation difference; C2 separately determines whether that relation is central or incidental.

For C2, MATERIAL and CRITICAL require a changed or unresolved core fact, event, identifiable entity or term, value, participant relation, logical condition, stance, or conclusion. Awkward wording or an incidental local difference in discourse, degree, quantification, or reference is NONE or MINOR when the same central claim remains clear; do not equate every S1-S4 semantic difference with consequential impact.

questions.question: Are the spans a plausible local alignment of the same ASR edit location, regardless of whether their meanings differ?

definitions.VALID: The spans occupy the same local edit position and their boundaries support comparison. A substitution may be VALID even when the two spans have very different meanings.
definitions.PARTIALLY_VALID: The spans broadly correspond, but one boundary includes or omits nearby material.
definitions.INVALID: The spans were paired from unrelated positions or the boundaries are so wrong that the highlighted local error is not the actual ASR edit. Do not choose INVALID merely because the meanings differ.
definitions.UNSCORABLE: There is insufficient information to judge alignment validity.

questions.question: Are the reference, hypothesis, and available context sufficient to judge the semantic consequence?

definitions.SCORABLE: The visible evidence supports a reliable consequence judgment.
definitions.UNSCORABLE: The reference is defective, required context is absent, or multiple materially different interpretations remain plausible.

questions.question: Does the error add, remove, or change a fact, event, action, state, predicate, or proposition?

definitions.NO_CHANGE: The proposition or event is preserved.
definitions.MINOR_FORM_CHANGE: Wording, fluency, discourse form, repetition, or grammar changes without changing the proposition. This includes a discourse marker, code-switched grammatical equivalent, repeated fragment, or recoverable grammatical omission when the complete sentence still expresses the same event and informative content.
definitions.SEMANTIC_CHANGE: A fact, event, action, state, predicate, informative object, or other propositional content is added, removed, replaced, or left incomplete. A deletion inside the same aligned content word or predicate counts when the resulting full hypothesis contains no complete recognized item. Do not infer truncation when adjacent or repeated material completes the expression, and do not mark SEMANTIC_CHANGE for awkward grammar, filler, synonym, paraphrase, or boundary spill when the complete sentence still expresses the same proposition.
definitions.UNCERTAIN: The evidence does not support a reliable choice.

questions.question: Does the error change an entity, attribute, professional term, number, time, date, unit, version, or quantity?

definitions.NO_CHANGE: The entity, attribute, term, or value is preserved.
definitions.MINOR_FORM_CHANGE: A recognized spelling, transliteration, abbreviation, spoken form, or established rendering differs while the hypothesis still uniquely identifies the same entity, professional term, attribute, or value. Phonetic closeness, small edit distance, or contextual guessability alone does not establish a recognized variant, especially for proper names and identifiers.
definitions.SEMANTIC_CHANGE: The identity, attribute, professional term, parameter, or value differs, is truncated into an incomplete item, or is no longer uniquely identifiable from the hypothesis. An altered proper name, technical term, identifier, or value is semantic unless the hypothesis itself supplies a recognized complete variant that uniquely preserves the same item.
definitions.UNCERTAIN: The evidence does not support a reliable choice.

questions.question: Does the error change clause type, question versus assertion force, negation, modality, certainty, condition, comparison, quantifier scope, tense, or completion status?

definitions.NO_CHANGE: Clause type, logical force, scope, and completion status are preserved.
definitions.MINOR_FORM_CHANGE: A surface, auxiliary, or grammatical form changes without changing clause type, logical force, scope, or completion status.
definitions.SEMANTIC_CHANGE: Question versus assertion force, negation, modality, certainty, condition, comparison, quantifier scope, tense, or completion status changes in the complete sentence. Require an actual change in interpretation; a contraction, auxiliary variant, or incidental degree nuance is not enough when the central claim retains the same force.
definitions.UNCERTAIN: The evidence does not support a reliable choice.

questions.question: Does the error change participant roles, subject/object, reference, causality, temporal relation, viewpoint attribution, or another semantic relation?

definitions.NO_CHANGE: Roles and semantic relations are preserved.
definitions.MINOR_FORM_CHANGE: The wording changes without changing an informative participant or relation. A recoverable subject ellipsis, agreement form, filler, or boundary artifact belongs here only when the complete sentence uniquely preserves the same participant, person, number, possession, and role.
definitions.SEMANTIC_CHANGE: A participant, role, referent, cause, temporal relation, viewpoint attribution, grammatical person, number, or possessor changes or becomes unresolved. Record a pronoun substitution as a relation change when it denotes a distinct participant or participant set; whether that difference is consequential belongs to C2, not S4.
definitions.UNCERTAIN: The evidence does not support a reliable choice.

questions.question: Using only the ASR hypothesis and available reader context, can a reasonable reader uniquely and reliably recover the original meaning?

definitions.FULLY_RECOVERABLE: The hypothesis and reader-visible context support one informative interpretation matching the intended meaning. This may include a discourse or grammatical variation, code-switched equivalent, conventional spoken form, ordinary homophone in a uniquely constraining conventional expression, or ellipsis whose participant remains uniquely fixed. A changed pronoun does not qualify when person, number, possessor, or specific referent remains different or unresolved. A proper name, technical term, identifier, or value must remain uniquely identified by a complete recognized form in the hypothesis; silent reference-based correction is not allowed.
definitions.PARTIALLY_RECOVERABLE: The broad event or topic is clear, but an informative predicate, entity, term, value, participant, logical condition, stance, or clause force remains unresolved. Context may suggest the missing detail without uniquely preserving it.
definitions.NOT_RECOVERABLE: The visible hypothesis supports a different informative interpretation or multiple materially different interpretations. An incomplete content word, different valid informative word, unrecognized proper-name spelling, corrupted technical term, identifier, or parameter counts as unrecovered when the hypothesis itself does not uniquely preserve the intended item.
definitions.UNSCORABLE: The context or intended meaning is too incomplete to assess recoverability.

boundary_examples: A sentence-final or boundary-local deletion that leaves an informative word visibly incomplete is not fully recoverable merely because its likely completion can be guessed.
A recognized transliteration or established spelling variant may be fully recoverable; a merely plausible phonetic spelling of a proper name is not enough.
An ordinary-word homophone can be fully recoverable when the complete hypothesis and a conventional collocation permit only the intended informative reading.

An omitted grammatical subject can be fully recoverable when the surrounding clause uniquely preserves who participates and what happened; a changed pronoun with a different person, number, or possessor is not repaired merely by knowing the topic.
Recovering only the topic while an informative term, identity, value, relation, clause force, or predicate remains uncertain is PARTIALLY_RECOVERABLE.

questions.question: How much would a reasonable reader's interpretation of the ASR hypothesis differ from the speaker's intended meaning?

definitions.NONE: The reader obtains the same informative interpretation; any difference is formal or fully recoverable from reader-visible evidence.
definitions.MINOR: A local difference is noticeable, but the same central claim remains clear. This includes discourse wording, awkward grammar, generic reference, recoverable subject omission, or an incidental degree or quantifier nuance that does not change the passage's central fact, event, entity, condition, stance, or conclusion. Recognizing only the broad topic is not enough when a core detail remains unresolved.
definitions.MATERIAL: A core fact, event, predicate, entity identity, key term, informative object or parameter, participant relation, logical condition, number, clause force, stance, or conclusion differs or remains unresolved for the reader. This includes an incomplete informative word and an unrecognized proper name or technical term when that item is needed for the sentence's core interpretation. Do not choose MATERIAL solely because S1-S4 records a real but incidental local difference.
definitions.CRITICAL: The error reverses a central conclusion, negation, key entity, responsibility, safety fact, or other high-risk meaning.
definitions.UNSCORABLE: The available evidence cannot support a reliable impact judgment.

boundary_examples: A discourse marker, filler, inflection, code-switched grammatical equivalent, conventional spoken form, generic pronoun, or recoverable ellipsis is NONE or MINOR when the same central claim remains clear.
An unresolved incomplete predicate or content word, entity identity, key term, value, or question-versus-assertion force is MATERIAL when it carries the sentence's central information.
A real difference in degree, quantification, reference, or grammar is MINOR when it is incidental and leaves the same central claim, stance, and conclusion clear.
Judge impact independently after S1-S4 and C1; neither SEMANTIC_CHANGE nor NOT_RECOVERABLE automatically implies MATERIAL.
